newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian cooling tower maker Hamon goes public.
newsitem.headline: Belgian cooling tower maker Hamon goes public.

text.p: Belgian Hamon, a producer of cooling systems and heat exchangers for power plants, will go public on a Brussels bourse crowded with new issues this month.

Hamon is not a household name, but in the world of electricity producers, the little Belgian multinational is well known. The group is world leader in the characteristic tall cooling towers adjoining power plants.

With the money from the 700 million franc ($20 million) initial public offering, Hamon will acquire Italian heat exchanger producer FBM Hudson, develop "dry" cooling systems and fund its expansion in Asia, Hamon said on Friday.
Hamon expects turnover to double from 1996's 9.06 billion ($253 million) francs to 18-20 billion ($532 million) on the back of growing environmental concern in emerging markets.

"People are starting to realise that they cannot just pump their electricity plant's cooling water into the river anymore, it kills the fish," Hamon chief executive Francis Lambilliotte told a news conference.
Hamon's main competitors are U.S. firm Marley and German firms Balcke-Durr and GEA.
Hamon is billing itself as a "green stock", which convinced two French investment funds specialised in environment and energy to take a minority stake in the company in April.

Euro-Environnement Investissement (which bought a 6.49 percent stake) and Electropar France SA (which bought 1.39 percent), both managed by a unit of French Caisse des Depots et Consignations, together subscribed to a 300 million Belgian franc capital increase prior to Hamon's IPO.
Both funds, in which French electricity producer Electricite de France is a shareholder, have agreed not to sell their shares before June 30, 1999.
Hamon's IPO is one of the few new listings on the Brussels bourse where the money raised will go solely to the company, and not to the pockets of existing shareholders.

After the IPO, Sopal International, a holding company owned by the Hamon and Lambilliotte families will hold 78.20 percent of Hamon, the investing public 14.69, and the two French funds will hold the rest.
Hamon & Cie (International) SA will offer 325,000 shares on the Brussels bourse at a price between 2,050 to 2,280 francs.
After the June 9-12 bookbuilding period, the price will be fixed on June 13. Subscriptions will run from June 13 to 20. The share will be quoted on the double-fixing cash market.

Christian De Marnix, chief investment banker at Paribas Bank Belgium which arranged the issue, said that a listing in France -- Hamon's biggest market, accounting for 28 percent of its sales -- had not been considered as this would have reduced liquidity in the share. But he added this may be possible later.

Paribas analyst Anne Soubrier said in a study that Hamon profits were disappointing in the 1992-95 period, but should be up sharply from 1997 onwards. "They are expected to double in 1998 and to increase by 30 percent per annum until 2001."
In 1996, Hamon earned a 99 million franc net profit on turnover of 9.06 billion, compared to 60 million in 1995 on turnover of 8.94 billion.
